pages.x: Beaten in the First World War, the Ottoman Empire lay at the mercy of the Allies. Their troops occupied Constantinople, and they planned to share out Anatolia itself. On 15 May 1919, with Allied backing, a Greek army landed at Smyrna, a city with a large Greek population.

Four days later Mustafa Kemal, the general who had held Gallipoli, landed at Samsun on the Black Sea, sent to keep order. Instead he rallied a resistance. At congresses in Erzurum and Sivas, nationalists swore to defend the Turkish lands as one, and in April 1920 they opened their own parliament in Ankara.

In August 1920 the sultan's government signed the Treaty of Sèvres. It left the Turks only part of Anatolia: Smyrna went to Greece to govern, the east to a new Armenia and a possible Kurdistan, and much of the south to French and Italian spheres. The parliament in Ankara refused it, and fought on.

In the autumn of 1920 the nationalists beat the Armenian republic in the east and took Kars. In the south, Turkish fighters drove the French out of Cilicia, and France made peace with Ankara in 1921. Soviet Russia sent gold and guns.

In the summer of 1921 the Greek army marched on Ankara. Kemal, given full command by the parliament, met it at the Sakarya River, less than a hundred kilometres from the capital. For 22 days the armies fought along a front of about a hundred kilometres, until the Greeks fell back, exhausted. Kemal was hailed as Gazi, the victorious.

On 26 August 1922 Kemal struck the Greek lines near Afyon. Within days the Greek army broke at Dumlupınar and fled for the coast, and on 9 September Turkish cavalry rode into Smyrna. His order to his troops became famous: "Armies, your first goal is the Mediterranean."

Days later a great fire swept through the Greek and Armenian quarters of Smyrna. Thousands were killed, and hundreds of thousands crowded onto the waterfront, desperate to escape, as Allied warships looked on. Who started the fire is still argued over; most historians outside Turkey blame Turkish soldiers.

Kemal sent İsmet Pasha, who had twice held the Greeks at İnönü, to make peace at Lausanne in Switzerland. Hard of hearing, he would, it is said, simply not hear the demands he disliked. After eight months, in July 1923, the Allies recognised Turkey over all Anatolia and eastern Thrace.

Greece and Turkey agreed to swap their minorities by religion. Over a million Orthodox Christians, most of whom had already fled, lost their homes in Turkey, and about 400,000 Muslims were sent from Greece to Turkey, leaving towns and villages where their families had lived for centuries.

pages.x: The parliament in Ankara had abolished the sultanate in November 1922, and the last sultan left on a British warship. On 29 October 1923 it proclaimed the Republic of Turkey, with Ankara as its capital and Mustafa Kemal as its first president.

Turks call it the War of Liberation, and its victory is the founding story of their republic. For Greeks it ended three thousand years of Greek life on the coast of Asia Minor, in what they call the Catastrophe. Under Kemal, the new Turkey set out to remake itself as a secular, Western-looking nation.
